name: shipping birds spring river bank Waal Zaltbommel Netherlands 1237 pm 260423_0099
description:
Heavy shipping traffic on the River Waal near Zaltbommel in the Netherlands. An inland vessel has just disappeared from the audio-visual feed. Here, the waves are lapping against the stone-reinforced bank. #1:28 Geese are flying in. #2:16 Waves from the river crash against the bow of the ship sailing downstream. It’s no longer in the port of Rotterdam. A moment later, you can hear the ship’s engines and the waves lapping against the bank. Then it goes quiet again for a moment. #6:21 There’s another small flock of geese. #9:02 A woman walking her dog says something briefly, but I can’t make it out. #9:56 Now a ship is coming upstream from the direction of Rotterdam. Once the ship has passed, it’s relatively quiet again, apart from the distant traffic noise from the A2 motorway.
About the picture The photo shows an old ferry landing. On the right is an old, somewhat dilapidated but still functioning government water level gauge. The microphone is positioned just behind the building, sheltered from the wind. Directly in front of you is the wide river, where an inland vessel is navigating against the strong current. On the left is the entrance to the town harbour, which is mainly used for pleasure boating. A tour boat is currently moored there. On the opposite side of the small harbour stands an old, dilapidated building. There are two cars on the quay. Slightly to the left of centre, next to the landing stage, is a water level gauge with a steel staircase about 3 metres high. Across the water, you can see the scenic floodplains with their trees and bushes. The sky is a clear blue.

At Pannerden, the bulk of the Rhine’s water leaves the main channel and flows westwards as the Waal towards the North Sea. The river flows past towns such as Nijmegen, Tiel and Zaltbommel, forming a central artery in the Dutch river system. Thanks to its high water discharge and wide navigable channel, the Waal has become the busiest inland waterway in Western Europe. Every day, hundreds of inland vessels pass through, transporting goods between Germany, the Netherlands and the port of Rotterdam. The river is therefore not only a natural feature but also an economic driver. Along its banks lie beautiful, expansive floodplains that provide space for high water and form an important nature reserve. Here, channels, grasslands and riverbanks alternate, creating a dynamic landscape that is constantly shaped by the river. Historically, the Waal has played a major role in the development of the region. The river determined where towns were established, how trade developed and where dykes had to be built. To this day, the Waal remains a defining factor in water management, shipping and nature conservation. name: River Maas March 8am Sunday 180408_1259.flac
description: Ambiance of a river on Sunday morning in March. Here, along this river the Maas, on a Sunday morning it is quiet. But, when you put your headphones on you hear many details. A sheep and a great spotted woodpecker indicating its territory. The dog and the roosters are also heard. Trains rush along the steel bridge to the city. Church bells in the surrounding villages, one later than the others, indicate the right time. Cows want to be milked. Even a bumblebee around. Crows and rooks always scratch here. The first traffic. Geese argue about a female. The first motorcyclist enjoys the view from the dike Dutch river dike. Later on, beautiful sound recordings will no longer be possible. After all, it is the first warm spring day and they will be flocking around in a couple of hours. The oystercatchers are twittering. They, like me, also have spring in mind. After 15 minutes and 40 seconds you hear how their singing starts slowly. Although you can not be here now, close your eyes and enjoy. That is what my distant family also regularly does. name: side channel river Waal Hurwenen Zaltbommel Netherlands 338 pm  260802_0149
description:
A summery and windy day by the side channel and ‘Kil van Hurwenen’ nature reserve, on the River Waal near Zaltbommel in the Netherlands. Many birds like Gulls and Terns in front. The humming of passing ships over the river on 500 metre.
About the picture From the bank, you look out over a tranquil stretch of water, a wide tributary of the river. The water is still and reflects the blue sky dotted with soft, white clouds. To the left lies a natural, somewhat untidy bank of sand and mud, where the branches of overhanging trees almost touch the water. On that left bank lies an old shipwreck. It has partly sunk into the sand and is clearly weathered by time and water. The wreck lies still and abandoned, a striking yet peaceful feature of the landscape. On the right-hand side, you can see a strip of land with dense vegetation: trees, bushes and grass running along the riverbank. Behind that strip lies another stretch of water, giving the landscape the appearance of a green embrace around the channel. In the distance, at the far left, lies the wide River Waal. You can recognise it by its open water surface, the wide horizon and the inland vessel just passing by.

About the shipwreck The wreck has been lying in the Kil since 1978, but possibly even earlier. The shipwreck in the Kil at Hurwenen is a steel ‘hevelaak’ (Hagenaar) named Henrica Maria. The ship, built for freight transport, had a hold with a fore and aft section and measures over 21 by 4 metres. The ship was equipped with a mast and boom with a unloading mechanism, as well as a side-thruster system powered by a diesel engine, but none of these components remain.
About the The Kil van Hurwenen The Kil van Hurwenen (also known as the Hurwenensche Uiterwaarden) is a nature reserve covering approximately 146 hectares in the floodplain of the Waal near the village of Hurwenen (municipality of Maasdriel). The area is still regularly flooded at high water and was formed when an old meander of the Waal was cut off from the river in 1639. In order to improve the river’s course, this bend in the Waal was cut off in 1639, leaving the Kil as a cut-off river branch. This was done by the river administrator of the time, who wanted to straighten the course of the Waal. For centuries, the area was used for haymaking and as pasture for livestock. In the 19th century, clay was extracted there for the brickworks. During high water, the area is still flooded with river water; work has also been carried out to improve the quality of the natural environment and water, including the construction of a parallel channel that flows alongside the main channel. The word ‘kil’ in ‘Kil van Hurwenen’ is Old Dutch for a water channel or stream carved out by flowing water.

name: Sunday May riverside Maas Bokhoven Netherlands 820 am 260524_0114
description:
It is an early Sunday morning on the edge of the floodplain of the River Meuse, near the village of Bokhoven in the Netherlands. #0:09 The finch is awake. It starts singing loudly. In the distance, the sound of traffic and shipping #0:36 I can see someone walking along the water’s edge with a dog, and you can hear the dog barking. #1:36 Flocks of starlings are calling and repeatedly taking flight from the tall grass of the floodplain. #2:32 Can you hear the cuckoo? It is a large bird that lays its egg in the nest of another species. When the chick hatches, it pushes the other chick out of the nest, and the often much smaller parents have to go to great lengths to feed their intruder. #3:55 The cockerel is late today. #4:01 Listen, the Egyptian goose is calling. In the Netherlands, it is an invasive species that is hunted. #5:20 Now the dove or pigeons are cooing too. #5:59 A pair of horses are neighing. #7:14 Someone has decided to start working with a chainsaw early. #7:44 A cyclist. #8:23 A young woman is doing her training lap on the paved cycle path. #8:34 The church bells of Ammerzoden and Bokhoven announce that it is half past seven. #8:44 Across the river, a horse is neighing. #9:30 Two ladies come speeding past on racing bikes, chatting away. #13:05 There go the starlings flying up from the fields. #13:48 And yet another group of cycling couples, the woman of whom says it’s ‘lovely here’. #14:21 The hoarse cries of two Egyptian geese, which are considered an invasive species in our country.
About the picture The photograph shows a typical Brabant river landscape: spacious, green, peaceful, and with a beautiful transition between the village and the countryside. In the foreground is the grassy embankment, with the photographer’s long shadow cast upon it. The embankment slopes gently down towards a wide green plain. Left a group of large trees and a small skate park and playground with concrete ramps. Behind them, a few houses from the village of Bokhoven are half-hidden amongst the greenery. On the right, the vast floodplain stretching towards the Meuse. In the distance, you can see the water glistening on the river. The sky is a clear blue with a few contrails.

name: birds floodplain - Meuse river - village Moordhuizen Netherlands  938 am 260601_0120
description:
Spring at the hallow waters of the river. A summer’s day in spring in the river floodplains. Teeming with insects and waterbirds. #1:39 #19:14 #20:15 Cars in the distance driving off the ferry. #6:00 #9:20 #23:42 #29:30 An aeroplane high up in the sky. #7:36 #12:47 Mute swans, with their characteristic wing beats, fly overhead. #15:00 A flock of greylag geese also flies overhead. #20:25 #28:11 A little later, more small flocks take off. #16:52 Nature lets out a good, long sigh. #19:21 A cargo ship creeps slowly past on the river. Even from a kilometre away, the ship’s engine can be heard clearly. 21:37 The clock at the church in the village of Lith or Lithoijen strikes ten o’clock.
About the picture You can see a parallel branch of the River Meuse, which serves as an additional floodplain. The sky is blue at the start of this summer’s day. Only a few scattered clouds herald an approaching deterioration in the weather within the next 24 hours. On the left, across the river, lies the village of Lith in North Brabant. You can also see large trees standing there to the right. These are ‘marker trees’ on the riverbank and used to serve as navigation aids for shipping. The river itself is not visible. However, the shallow side channel of the river, where countless birds nest, is visible. The terrain is gently sloping and is now the domain of cattle that graze here all year round. The floodplain where we are is covered with grass and low shrubs. There are a few trees for the cattle, so they can take shelter.

About the environment The River Meuse flows through this area. We are now on the north bank of the river near Moordhuizen, a hamlet in the province of Gelderland. This audio recording was made at a lake that serves as a flood retention area during high water and as a breeding ground for many birds, amongst other things.
